title: Things to Say to High-Achieving Students If You Are Worried They Want to Move On
author: Barton, Craig
summary: Barton revisits his long-running critique of differentiation, this time focused specifically on the modelling phase of a lesson. He argues that pulling high-achieving students out of whole-class modelling early is a mistake, since after only one or two examples neither teacher nor student has enough evidence to know how secure that understanding really is. Rather than accelerating those students onto independent practice, he offers four phrases teachers can use to keep them engaged and thinking during modelling: framing overlearning as valuable, normalizing the discomfort of struggle, warning them they may be asked to explain their reasoning, and challenging them to prepare to teach a struggling peer. The piece closes by reaffirming that real differentiation should wait until later in the learning episode, once there is genuine evidence of which students have actually secured the knowledge.
points: Barton argues the modelling phase is the worst time to differentiate, because a student getting an early answer right is not yet evidence that their understanding is secure.

He supplies four ready-to-use phrases for keeping high-achievers engaged without pulling them out of whole-class modelling: overlearning is good, enjoy the struggle, show me you understand, and can you help someone who doesn't understand it yet.
The 'explain it to someone else' phrase is framed as the hardest test of understanding, doubling as both extension and peer support.
Differentiation, in Barton's framing, belongs later in the learning episode once there is real evidence of which students have secured the knowledge, not during initial exposure to it.
quotes: But of all the times to differentiate, the modelling phase is the worst. When we are introducing our students to a new idea, do we really have enough evidence to decide that one group of students gets it and so can crack on whilst we provide more examples for others?
Differentiation can come later on in the learning episode when both we and the students have more evidence of how secure their knowledge is.
Overlearning is good! We want to practice this not until we get it right, but until we can’t get it wrong. So, let’s do another.
Enjoy the feeling of understanding something. There will be plenty of times when you struggle - after all, everyone struggles - and that might not feel so good.

Show me you really understand this. I can see that you can get the right answer, but in a moment I am going to need to know exactly how to get there, why we do this and not that, and I might just come to you to find out, so keep listening and thinking.
Can you help someone who doesn’t understand it yet? It is one thing being able to get a question correct, and it is even harder to understand how you got the answer.
These suggestions might just keep your high-achieving students engaged enough to ensure their understanding is as secure as we need it to be.
